Source Integrity Notes

  • Year labels follow the uploaded filenames/cohort labels. The printed calendar dates in some PDFs are earlier than the cohort label.
  • 2028 source: numbering jumps from Q64 to Q68 and ends at Q99. Q65–67 and Q100 are not present in the uploaded PDF and were not invented.
  • 2025 source: Q89 is not present in the uploaded PDF and was not invented.
  • 2026 source: the PDF itself states that no department feedback was given and that answers and rationales came from research using transes and reference books.
  • Historical answer keys are preserved exactly. When a key conflicts with its rationale or another version, the family displays a visible warning rather than silently correcting it.

Physician-Patient Communication Goals
Same Concept, New FramingPhysician-Patient Communication9 appearances2025 · 2026
⌄
Master Rule
Distinguish the recurring communication goals: gathering information, providing information, responding to emotions, enabling treatment-related behavior, and fostering the relationship.
Examiner Pattern
The same small set of goals returns with different physician statements, so the distractors themselves are a recurring knowledge set.
SourceQuestion and Complete ChoicesKeyChoice-by-Choice Rationale
2025 Q1PDF page 1
Match the statement with the physician-patient communication goals: “How did your cough start and what medication did you take?”
A. Providing information
B. Responding to emotions
C. Enabling treatment related behavior
D. Gathering information✓
D
A. Incorrect
Explains the problem and the approach to diagnosis or treatment, gives clear instructions, and helps the patient understand and use information.
B. Incorrect
Acknowledges and explores emotions, expresses empathy or reassurance, and helps the patient deal with emotional consequences of illness.
C. Incorrect
Assesses readiness to change, elicits goals and decisions, gives advice, and agrees on next steps.
D. Correct
Uses open-ended questions, elicits the full description and patient perspective, clarifies information, and asks about additional concerns. This is the keyed choice in this source version.

Temporal Profile Patterns
Same Concept, New FramingHistory Taking / Temporal Profile / Symptom Analysis9 appearances2025 · 2026 · 2027
⌄
Master Rule
Know the visual patterns for gradual/progressive, acute, intermittent, remittent, recurrent, and periodic courses. The exams repeatedly ask students to translate a plotted symptom course into its descriptive term.
Examiner Pattern
These are image-based choice variants. The wording changes less than the plotted temporal pattern.
SourceQuestion and Complete ChoicesKeyChoice-by-Choice Rationale
2025 Q31PDF page 5
Match the temporal profile diagram with its corresponding descriptive equivalence:
A. Gradual onset✓
B. Acute onset
C. Recurrent
D. Remittent
A
A. Correct
A symptom course that develops progressively from baseline rather than appearing abruptly. This is the keyed choice in this source version.
B. Incorrect
A symptom course that begins abruptly.
C. Incorrect
A symptom pattern that returns after a period of improvement or absence.
D. Incorrect
A course that improves but does not fully return to baseline.
Original PDF Rationale

Cardinal PE Maneuver Sequence by Organ System
Same Concept, New FramingComplete PE / General Survey / Vital Signs7 appearances2025 · 2026 · 2027 · 2028
⌄
Master Rule
Most systems follow inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation. The abdomen is the classic exception, where auscultation precedes percussion and palpation. Organ-specific questions test this sequence from different directions.
SourceQuestion and Complete ChoicesKeyChoice-by-Choice Rationale
2025 Q36PDF page 5
What is the proper sequence in assessing the liver?
A. Directly auscultate, then palpate then percuss
B. Directly auscultate, then percussion and then palpate
C. Inspect, then palpate then percuss
D. Inspect, then percussion and then palpate✓
D
A. Incorrect
Assess the liver and spleen by percussion and then palpation. Percuss the liver
B. Incorrect
Tapping the body surface to interpret underlying density or resonance.
C. Incorrect
Assess the liver and spleen by percussion and then palpation. Percuss the liver
D. Correct
Tapping the body surface to interpret underlying density or resonance. This is the keyed choice in this source version.
Original PDF Rationale

Comprehensive vs Focused Physical Assessment
Inverted / Choice VariantsComplete PE / General Survey / Vital Signs7 appearances2025 · 2026 · 2027 · 2028
⌄
Master Rule
Comprehensive assessment is broad and especially useful for new patients, health promotion, relationship building, and identifying or ruling out physical causes. Focused assessment is problem-oriented and useful for repeated follow-up.

D. Incorrect

Biopsychosocial Communication Style
Direct & Near RepeatsPhysician-Patient Communication4 appearances2025 · 2026 · 2027 · 2028
⌄
Master Rule
Biopsychosocial communication is patient-centered. It recognizes concerns and emotions, elicits personal context, and facilitates the patient’s story. The uploaded exams repeatedly label it the gold standard or best practice.
Examiner Pattern
The examiner alternates between asking for the defining feature and presenting a clinical response that acknowledges emotion while still investigating symptoms.

Myopia, Presbyopia, and Near-vs-Distance Vision
Same Concept, New FramingOphthalmology4 appearances2027 · 2028
⌄
Master Rule
Myopia causes worse distance vision with relatively better near vision. Presbyopia causes progressive difficulty with near work in older adults. Asking whether near or distance vision is better helps localize the refractive problem.
SourceQuestion and Complete ChoicesKeyChoice-by-Choice Rationale
2027 Q82PDF page 14
A 19 year old college student came due to blurred vision at distance. During physical examination, he tends to move closer to the visual acuity chart to see the biggest letters. Which among the choices is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Myopia✓
B. Hyperopia
C. Presbyopia
D. Anisometropia
A
A. Correct
Nearsightedness. Distance vision is worse because light focuses in front of the retina. This is the keyed choice in this source version.
B. Incorrect
Farsightedness. Near work is typically more difficult because the optical system focuses behind the retina without accommodation.
C. Incorrect
Age-related loss of near focusing ability, producing progressive difficulty with close work.
D. Incorrect
Anisometropia means unequal refractive power between the two eyes. It is different from simple myopia causing poor distance vision.
Original PDF Rationale
Patient has difficulty of distance vision (nearsightedness) Difficulty with close work, suggestive of hyperopria (farsightedness) The physiologic change in accommodation power in the eyes in advancing age Difference in the refractive power of the eyes
2028 Q57PDF page 13
A 52/M complained of gradual difficulty reading fine print, but can see distant objects clearly. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Myopia
B. Hyperopia
C. Presbyopia✓
D. Astigmatism
C
A. Incorrect
Nearsightedness. Distance vision is worse because light focuses in front of the retina.
B. Incorrect
Farsightedness. Near work is typically more difficult because the optical system focuses behind the retina without accommodation.
C. Correct
Age-related loss of near focusing ability, producing progressive difficulty with close work. This is the keyed choice in this source version.
D. Incorrect
Astigmatism causes blurred or distorted vision.
Original PDF Rationale
Myopia (nearsightedness) is likely if the person needs to move nearer to see the object clearly. Hyperopia (farsightedness) is likely if the person needs to move a little backward to refocus the object in the retina. Presbyopia (aging vision) is associated with difficulties in viewing objects at a close distance. Astigmatism causes blurred or distorted vision. Reference trans/book: 2028 LE 1 Trans 4: Ophthalmologic History Taking and PE

2028 Q75PDF page 16
Why is it important to ask if vision improves with near or far distance?
A. To detect glaucoma
B. To determine surgical urgency
C. To check for accommodation amplitude
D. To check for types of errors of refraction✓
D
A. Incorrect
Progressive optic-nerve disease associated in the uploaded exam with peripheral visual-field loss that can progress to tunnel vision.
B. Incorrect
Surgical urgency (e.g., for cataract) depends on overall functional
C. Incorrect
Increases lens convexity for near focus and occurs with convergence and miosis in the near response.
D. Correct
refractive errors (e.g., myopia vs hyperopia/presbyopia). This is the keyed choice in this source version.
Original PDF Rationale
Glaucoma causes optic nerve damage and visual field loss, rather than a simple difference in clarity between near and far. Surgical urgency (e.g., for cataract) depends on overall functional impairment, symptoms and exam, not solely whether vision is better at near or distance. Accommodation amplitude must be measured with specific tests, and a casual near-far comparison is an imprecise clue at best. Asking whether vision improves at near or far directly distinguishes refractive errors (e.g., myopia vs hyperopia/presbyopia). Reference trans/book: 2028 LE 1 - Trans 4: Ophthalmologic History Taking and PE

B. Enhance the visibility of subtle chest wall abnormalities by casting shadows
C. Standardize the examination procedure for reproducibility
D. Assist in detecting abnormal heart sounds such as murmurs on auscultation
A
A. Correct
Tangential light is directed at a low angle to create shadows that make subtle contours, pulsations, elevations, and depressions easier to see, including the JVP and apical impulse. This is the keyed choice in this source version.
B. Incorrect
where shadows are reduced and subtle undulations
C. Incorrect
The low angle is used to enhance visibility of surface movement and contour, not primarily to standardize the procedure.
D. Incorrect
Listening to body sounds, usually with a stethoscope.
Original PDF Rationale
Tangential lighting involves positioning the light source at a low angle as to increase shadows. This would allow subtle details or movements to be observed. Tangential lighting is best for inspecting the jugular venous pulse, thyroid gland, and apical impulse of the heart. Reference trans/book: 2027/2028 - Overview of Complete PE/General Survey/Vital Signs

Original PDF Rationale
Ignoring or suppressing emotions leaves the patient feeling unheard and powerless. Empowerment requires validating feelings to support coping and trust. Patient-centered communication broadens the focus to include psychosocial context, values, and concerns. Limiting interaction to the “chief complaint” disempowers the patient. Empowering patients means encouraging them to share their story, priorities, and goals. This aligns with the communication goals of gathering information, decision-making, and empowering the patient. One of the goals is to provide information clearly and involve the patient in decision-making. Obscuring reasoning erodes trust and fosters dependency rather than empowerment. Many patients with chronic illness and new alarming symptoms (like coughing blood) may feel fear, anxiety, or denial. This can prevent them from disclosing the full extent of symptoms (e.g., duration, severity, lifestyle factors). This is a real patient barrier, because emotional distress may block open communication and make history-taking incomplete This represents a physician bias more than a patient barrier. Physicians may stereotype long-term smokers with COPD, assuming their illness is “self-inflicted” and thereby unconsciously neglecting or overlooking new red flags A long history of COPD, smoking, family history of cancer complicates the clinical picture. However, while it makes diagnosis more challenging, it is not a barrier created by the patient himself; it’s a clinical complexity. Older age does not automatically make a patient unreliable. Unless he has cognitive decline or dementia (not mentioned in the case), he can provide accurate history. Assuming that elderly patients are unreliable is an ageist misconception, not a true barrier here. Reference trans/book: 📖(2028) Physician-Patient Communication

Original PDF Rationale
Bronchial Breath Sounds: These are normally heard over the trachea and manubrium. They have a high pitch and are louder during expiration compared to inspiration. Bronchovesicular Breath Sounds: These are normally heard over the main bronchi and are a mix of bronchial and vesicular sounds, with equal inspiratory and expiratory phases. Vesicular Breath Sounds: These are normally heard over the lung fields and have a soft, low pitch with a longer inspiratory phase than expiratory phase. Bronchophony: This is not a type of breath sound but rather a term used to describe an increased clarity of spoken voice sounds when auscultating the lungs, indicating possible lung consolidation.

Used in tracheoesophageal puncture/prosthesis for voice restoration. Used in ophthalmology to visualize the anterior chamber of the eye. Device for emergency airway management and ventilation. A pneumatic bulb is used to introduce positive and negative pressure to the ear using specific examinations. It is used to evaluate the movement of the tympanic membrane. Original PDF Rationale
Causes monocular vision loss, typically affecting central vision, and does not impact the posterior visual pathway. Involves inflammation of the optic nerve, leading to central or monocular vision loss, not posterior pathway defects. Causes monocular visual deficits before the optic chiasm, unlikely to affect the posterior pathway. Often affects the posterior visual pathway, leading to homonymous hemianopia or other binocular visual field defects, making it the most likely cause of posterior pathway visual field defects.

Original PDF Rationale
[MED]-1.03-Overview of Complete PE/General Survey/Vital Signs When you percuss the abdomen, especially if you’re in the bowel loops and it is air-filled, it usually elicits a tympanic sound. If you percuss the lungs, you would hear a resonant sound. If you percuss a solid organ (ie. liver), you will hear dullness.

A. Incorrect
Dullness: This sound indicates the presence of fluid or solid matter, often found
B. Incorrect

C. Incorrect

Tympanitic: This sound is characterized by a hollow, drum-like quality and is This is the keyed choice in this source version.
Original PDF Rationale
Tympanitic: This sound is characterized by a hollow, drum-like quality and is typically heard over air-filled structures, such as the stomach and intestines when they are empty. Resonance: This is a normal sound over healthy lung tissue, indicating air presence, but is not specifically associated with the stomach. Dullness: This sound indicates the presence of fluid or solid matter, often found over the liver or when the lungs are filled with fluid (like in pneumonia). Stridor: This is not a percussion note but rather a high-pitched wheezing sound that indicates airway obstruction.
